As of 345 AM Thursday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... Shallow and isolated convection brings negligible 
rain amounts today, with shower and storm chances and coverage 
increasing tonight.

Aloft, the shortwave responsible for the rain currently across the 
wrn Piedmont, should lift nnewd out of the area this morning, while 
the positively tilted trough axis sharpens as it approaches from the 
west. While one s/w embedded in the trough is expected to weaken as 
it moves ewd across the cntl Plains and into the mid-MS Valley today 
and tonight, a pair of nrn stream shortwaves will interact over the 
Great Lakes, forming a closed low over the Great Lakes by Fri morn. 
At the surface, the ridge axis extending wwd into the region from a 
high north of Bermuda will get shunted to the ese, along the 
Southeast US and mid-Atlantic coasts tonight as a cold front 
approaches and moves into the area from the west. Expect increased 
advection of warm, moist air, from both the Gulf ahead of the front 
approaching from the west and from the Atlantic in return flow 
around the high north of Bermuda. 

Aside from perhaps a weak mid-level disturbance lifting into the 
area later this aft/eve, there will be a lack in mid/upr level 
forcing for convection today, however forecast soundings off the 
HRRR and RAP do show SBCAPE increasing to 500-1200 J/Kg (highest 
over the wrn Piedmont) through the day and into the evening. While 
an isolated shower or storm is possible today, duration and 
intensity may be limited. Chances, coverage, and intensity should 
increase tonight. 

Temperature forecast is a bit challenging in the west, dependent 
upon cloud cover and rainfall, but with sly flow advecting 
relatively warm air into the area, still expect well above normal 
temperatures. Highs ranging from low/mid 70s NW to low/mid 80s SE 
and lows tonight in the low to mid 60s. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... Showers and thunderstorms will continue Friday 
within a pre-frontal moist axis over cntl NC, with a Marginal risk 
of a few severe storms in the Sandhills and Coastal Plain midday 
through afternoon. 

GOES-E water vapor satellite data indicate a mid/upr-level cyclone 
now over the CO/NM border and vicinity may already be in the process 
of shearing and deamplifying ewd across the cntl and srn High Plains 
this morning; and the models indicate it will further do so and 
become an open wave trough by the time it reaches the Mid-South by 
12Z Fri. That feature is then forecast to rapidly lift newd and 
across the OH and TN Valleys and Middle Atlantic through Fri night. 
Related modest, 40-60 meter 500 mb height falls, and 40-50 kts of 
swly 500 mb flow, will overspread cntl NC on Fri, as the strongest 
flow and forcing for ascent otherwise pass just to the northwest and 
along or in the immediate lee of the cntl Appalachians. 

At the surface, a lead, srn stream cold front was evident in surface 
observational and radar data this morning across nwrn GA, e-cntl 
through s-cntl AL, and the far wrn FL panhandle. It stretched swwd 
from a ~1011 mb triple point-like wave over nrn GA (where MRMS data 
indicate almost 8" of rain fell and necessitated an earlier Flash 
Flood Emergency over Gilmer and Fanin Co.). That frontal wave and 
inflection point in surface theta-e was preceded by a maritime 
Tropical warm front that stretched sewd invof the Savannah Basin, 
along a confluence axis and near the 67-68F isodrosotherms. 
Continued sely through sly flow across the Carolinas will cause the 
warm front to effectively retreat nwwd and into the srn 
Appalachians, with a related moist sector characterized by mostly 
mid 60s F (to locally 67-68 F surface dewpoints) that will 
overspread cntl NC through 12Z Fri. Meanwhile, a nrn stream cold 
front arced from a ~996 mb cyclone over Lk Superior swd and across 
Lk Erie and OH. While this front will make steady ewd progress 
across the nrn Middle Atlantic, it will slow as it progresses into 
the Blue Ridge later tonight. The front, or at least an effective 
one that will likely serve as the wrn bound of the pre-frontal moist 
and instability axis, with developing nwly flow and dry air 
advection behind it, will then move ewd and across cntl and ern NC 
through the day Fri. This effective front may become strengthened by 
diabatic cooling and outflow from waves of convection tracking along 
and just behind it through the morning to midday hours, which at 
this time appears favored over the Piedmont. REFS members are in 
relatively good agreement regarding the development of deeper 
convection along or just ahead of the effective front as it 
progresses through the Sandhills and Coastal Plain during the 
afternoon.
